beats.spoken: In the EU, one single sentence decides what legally counts as a cosmetic.
The EU cosmetics regulation starts with the place. A cosmetic is applied externally to skin, hair, nails, lips and external intimate areas, or to the teeth and the lining of the mouth.

rows.text: teeth and lining of the mouth

beats.spoken: Then comes the purpose: cleaning, perfuming, changing the appearance, protecting, keeping in good condition, or correcting body odours. And that has to be the exclusive or main purpose. So perfume, make-up and toothpaste can all count as cosmetics.
In the US, the idea is similar but built differently. There, intended use decides. If a product claims to treat a disease or to affect how the body works, it becomes a drug.
So healing is not on the list of cosmetic purposes. A cream may care for your skin and protect it. A promise to heal is something else.

rows.text: a promise to heal: something else

beats.spoken: For you, that means: check what a product is meant for. If it says cleanse or care, it's a cosmetic. If it sounds like a treatment, ask what is really meant.
Read the purpose first, then apply. Beauty knowledge, clearly explained: follow Dewlane.
